Ruby phones his friend Breck Wall at a Galveston number, his last known long-distance call before shooting Oswald.
Joseph Milteer and informant William Somersett check into a hotel in Columbia, S.C., to meet Klan representatives about Milteer's new party.
Dr. Humes certifies that he burned "certain preliminary draft notes" of the autopsy report and sent all other papers to higher authority.

In a second certificate, Humes says all working papers stayed in his custody and the notes and draft went to Capt. Stover at 5 PM on November 24. He later says he copied the bloodstained notes and burned them so they would not fall into the wrong hands, and that he did not see the X-rays until about midnight or the photographs until years later.
Nicaraguan Gilberto Alvarado tells the U.S. Embassy in Mexico City he saw Cubans pay Oswald $6,500 to kill Kennedy; the story is later discredited.
Hoover urges that Oswald be transferred secretly; Parkland is told to be ready for an emergency.

The Secret Service traces "Lt. J. Evans" and "Sgt. Robert Hidell," references on Oswald's Reily job application. Naval Intelligence finds one possible Lt. John Evans and no Marine named Hidell, the closest being a John R. Heindel.

Anonymous callers warn the Dallas FBI and the sheriff's office that Oswald will be killed during the transfer; a switchboard operator later identifies the voice as Ruby's. Shanklin cannot reach Curry until 8:15, and plans do not change.

Johnson meets Ambassador Lodge on Vietnam. National Security Action Memorandum 273, dated November 26, follows; the chronology says it reversed Kennedy's withdrawal plan and set the course for escalation, a reading historians dispute.

McNamara later writes that Johnson told Lodge on November 24 he wanted to win the war and put military operations ahead of reform. In Columbia, Milteer tells Somersett over breakfast that Oswald "doesn't know anything."
UPI reporter Terrance McGarry's wife gets him up, saying he would never forgive himself if Oswald were shot and he had known it was coming.

TV cameraman Stephen Alexander says he was in the basement from now until the shooting and was never asked for identification; newscaster Ed Haddad says anyone could move freely through the building all weekend.
Shanklin finally reaches Curry with the threat.
Ruby's housekeeper Elnora Pitts calls his apartment as usual; a man who says he is Ruby answers, but does not sound like him and knows nothing of the arrangement.
Sheriff Decker leaves the transfer to Curry, who decides police will handle it and agrees with Batchelor and Stevenson to use an armored truck and a planned route.
In Columbia, Milteer returns with coffee and a handful of change, as if after a long-distance call, and tells Somersett Oswald has said nothing and will say nothing.
Senior officers issue detailed orders for the transfer.
Police clear and search the basement: guards at both ramps and the five doorways, Sgt. Patrick Dean's team checking rafters, ducts, rooms and cars, elevators locked or moved.

ABC's William Lord says he took a public elevator into the basement unchallenged. Of some 44 newsmen present, 14 say their credentials were not checked, nearly a third, which Sylvia Meagher says the Warren Report plays down.
Plano preacher Ray Rushing says he spoke with Ruby in a police headquarters elevator.

Hoover tells Johnson the Mexico City voice on the tapes is not Oswald's, suggesting a second person at the Soviet Embassy, and that the case is not yet strong enough to convict. The impersonation is kept to a handful of officials. The Secret Service holds Marina and Marguerite Oswald and the children at a Dallas motel.
Karen Carlin phones Ruby at his apartment.
Curry tells the press Oswald will go by armored truck. When it arrives about 11:07, Fritz objects and urges an unmarked police car; the truck becomes a decoy.
Capt. O.A. Jones has detectives form two lines along the passage for the transfer.

Fritz finishes questioning. Oswald chooses a black sweater; Secret Service Inspector Thomas Kelley says Oswald told him he would talk with his attorney present. Ruby parks across from the Western Union office, leaving $1,000, his keys and his dog in the car and carrying his revolver and $2,000.
Officer William "Blackie" Harrison is seen coming up from the subbasement, later saying he went for cigars; it has been suggested he tipped off Ruby by phone.
At Western Union, Ruby wires $25 to Karen Carlin in Fort Worth, then heads to the police building.
Ruby's roommate George Senator reportedly calls attorney Jim Martin from the Eat Well Cafe, minutes before the shooting, asking him to represent Ruby.

Carlin later tells the FBI, frightened, that she believed Oswald, Ruby and others plotted the assassination and she would be killed for talking. Reports of her death conflict; some say she later resurfaced.
Ruby's later lawyer Tom Howard enters, watches Oswald step off the jail elevator, says "That's all I wanted to see," and leaves.

Curry stays in his office to take a call from Mayor Cabell. A reporter notices Lt. George Butler visibly trembling. Sgt. Patrick Dean, who knew Ruby and was in charge of basement security, later fails a polygraph whose records disappear.
The money order is time-stamped four minutes before the shooting; some researchers argue Oswald was moved only once Ruby was in place.

A reserve officer, Harold Holly, reports another reserve officer told him he saw or admitted Ruby wearing a press badge; Holly names William Newman, whom Warren counsel Burt Griffin calls a liar to his face. Detective Jim Leavelle says Fritz ordered the move after conferring with FBI and Secret Service officials.
Oswald is taken down by elevator. Access to the basement is by two ramps and five doors; the Warren Commission has doubts about one door.
UPI's McGarry, at the foot of the Main Street ramp, says no one came down it in the five minutes before the shooting; cab driver Harry Tasker, watching the top of the ramp, says the same.
Tasker tells the FBI no one resembling Ruby went in.

As Lt. Pierce's car exits up the Main Street ramp, Ruby is said to slip down past it; Officer R.E. Vaughan, guarding the ramp, denies it. A WBAP employee says he saw Ruby on the ramp; a reserve sergeant's sighting may have been a TV newsman.
NBC executive Robert Kintner chooses to air the transfer live, so the shooting is televised; he later joins Johnson's staff.
Oswald enters, handcuffed to Leavelle, with Graves, Fritz, Swain and Montgomery; all but Fritz have known Ruby for years, as do dozens of officers present. No one spots him.
TV lights blind the escort; no one walks in front of Oswald. A car horn sounds twice. Ruby stands behind Officer Harrison, whom he has known eleven years. On the tape, Oswald seems to glance at Ruby.
Ruby lunges forward with the pistol; Detective Combest sees him coming but cannot reach him.

Ruby shoots Oswald on live NBC television, the first murder broadcast live. The bullet tears through major vessels and several organs. Officers give him artificial respiration, the worst treatment for such a wound. Combest testifies that Oswald, asked for a statement, only shook his head.
Combest's testimony about seeking a dying declaration does not appear in the Warren Report.
Leavelle rides in the ambulance and has the bullet marked by a nurse at Parkland for evidence.
Of 25 Dallas homicide detectives, only seven had been on duty November 22.
Mobster John Roselli later tells Jack Anderson the underworld feared Oswald would talk and ordered Ruby to silence him.
Johnson aide George Reedy at first mistakes the broadcast for an old gangster film.

Johnson tells Robert Kennedy they must act, as it is hurting America's image; RFK asks Walter Sheridan to look into Ruby. CIA official Desmond FitzGerald is said by his wife to have wept and said, "Now we'll never know."
Ruby later says that only someone in the police could have timed it so precisely.
The Warren Commission finds no suspicious ties between Ruby and police; Seth Kantor writes that from Sunday afternoon no Dallas policeman would admit knowing him.
After Mass in the East Room, Mrs. Kennedy asks to see the President's body.
With Robert Kennedy, she views him in the East Room and cuts a lock of his hair.
Surgery to save Oswald begins at Parkland.
Robert Kennedy closes the casket for the last time. In Dallas, Detective Guy Rose obtains a warrant to search Ruby's apartment.
Detectives search it from about 1 to 2 PM; no photographs are taken.
Networks report Oswald in critical condition.
Within half an hour Ruby tells four officers he came down the Main Street ramp, but none reports it for days, and he refuses to tell FBI agent Hall how he got in.
Dr. Charles Crenshaw later writes that Johnson phoned the operating room demanding a deathbed confession from Oswald.
Agnes Meyer asks Bill Walton whether the U.S. has become a banana republic. Mrs. Kennedy and the children watch the casket leave the White House for the Capitol Rotunda.
Mrs. Kennedy enters the Rotunda, staying twenty-two minutes.
Marina views her husband's body. She later tells a French journalist she had two husbands: Lee, a kind father, and "Harvey Oswald," the assassin.
Mortician Paul Groody notes neither the mastoidectomy scar in Oswald's Marine records nor scars from his 1957 arm wound.

Gary Mack says Dr. Carl Dockery took about 150 photographs at Oswald's autopsy, confiscated and never seen again. Deputy Attorney General Katzenbach drafts a proposal for a presidential commission. Agent Hosty is ordered to destroy Oswald's note, and Humes burns his original notes.
Mrs. Kennedy and Caroline kneel at the catafalque.
Hoover tells the White House his main concern is issuing something to convince the public Oswald is the real assassin, and orders Shanklin to clean up Oswald's Dallas FBI file.
Stripper Janet Conforto ("Jada") gives TV interviews about Ruby, then tells the FBI she never saw Oswald with him.

Eugene Rostow urges Bill Moyers to set up a commission of distinguished citizens. In New Orleans, lawyer G. Wray Gill tells Ferrie's roommate Layton Martens that Oswald was carrying a library card in Ferrie's name and offers to represent Ferrie.
No library card appears in the police inventory of Oswald's effects, yet Marina is later asked whether she knows David Ferrie.

Jack Martin tells a friend of New Orleans prosecutor Herman Kohlman that Ferrie and Oswald knew each other from the Civil Air Patrol, that Ferrie trained him with a scoped rifle, and that he heard them discuss killing Kennedy.
Ferrie learns he is being accused, heads home, and on Gill's advice spends the night at Southeastern Louisiana University in Hammond.

Fritz questions Ruby with FBI agent Hall present. Fritz writes that Ruby said he came down the Main Street ramp; Hall says Ruby would not say how or when he entered. The Commission accepts Hall's version.
Rusk, Ball and McNamara leave a meeting with Johnson; the rest of his log is mostly condolences.
Aristotle Onassis visits the White House as Mrs. Kennedy's private guest.
Hoover tells Johnson aide Walter Jenkins the FBI report should go to the Attorney General, leaving the President to decide what to release.
Hoover's memo for the record: nothing more on the Oswald case "except that he is dead."
Hoover sends Robert Kennedy an FBI wiretap transcript attributing a crude remark about Mrs. Kennedy to Martin Luther King (per Hersh, Bobby and J. Edgar).

An anonymous caller tells the FBI Oswald had a rifle scope mounted at the Irving Sports Shop. At dinner, Abe Fortas advises Johnson against a presidential commission. Johnson's advisers agree that some process must convince the public Oswald was the assassin, as commentators begin to voice doubt.
